claims.text: The starting CoCrFeMnNi alloy is single-phase FCC.
Atomic size misfits produce pronounced or severe lattice distortion in CoCrFeMnNi.
CoCrFeMnNi exhibits simultaneously high strength and ductility at elevated strain rates.
Spatial variation in lattice distortion creates heterogeneous dislocation-pinning sites.
Under dynamic loading, heterogeneous pinning sites cause intermittent dislocation depinning followed by rapid repinning.
Intermittent depinning and repinning produces burst-like dislocation activity and a self-regulating strain-hardening response.
At low strain rates, dislocations in the alloy move relatively uniformly and gradually without pronounced bursts.
At high strain rates, severe lattice distortion generates heterogeneous local pinning forces.
Intermittent dislocation motion enhances energy dissipation and dynamic hardening.
The proposed self-regulating dislocation response contributes causally to both enhanced strength and enhanced ductility.
The proposed comparison spans room-temperature strain rates from approximately 10^-3 s^-1 to 10^3 s^-1.
In situ high-speed TEM measurements will be compared with quasi-static and high-rate mechanical tests to relate dislocation behavior to mechanical response.
High-rate loading will produce a higher strain-hardening rate than quasi-static loading.
High-rate loading will produce burst-like or avalanche-like dislocation activity relative to quasi-static loading.
Dislocation velocity distributions and activation volumes will vary with strain rate.
High-rate loading will generate transient local strain-field changes observable by TEM and correlated with bulk mechanical behavior.
The hypothesis should apply to significantly lattice-distorted, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi at room temperature.
Lower lattice misfit or extreme temperatures may change the applicability of the proposed mechanism by altering dislocation mechanisms.

The hypothesis is falsified if dislocation velocity distributions and activation volumes remain invariant across strain rates and dynamic strain hardening does not differ from the quasi-static response.
